image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Stacked area chart (stream/stacked percentage area chart).

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Uses **stacking** of colored areas to show parts of a whole over time.  
- Single panel; **no faceting** or small multiples.  
- Areas appear normalized to represent **percent share** of total electricity production.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (2001–2023) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percentage of power produced | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; stacked area height/thickness |
| Energy source | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue; separate stacked area bands; text labels inside areas |
| Coal | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |
| Natural gas | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |
| Nuclear | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |
| Hydroelectric | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |
| Wind | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |
| Solar | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |
| Petroleum | Categorical/nominal | One colored stacked area band; label |

Visible annotations:
- Percentage labels at the left and right edges are **text labels** showing values for selected sources at the start/end of the period.

comments.raw_comment: This graph showcases what percentage of power was produced and by what way from the year 2001 to 2003.  Something interesting I learned from this graph is how the proportion of each shape corresponding to the different types of energies changes along with its impact or percentage in that year.  So as the percentage of power from a energy source decreases so does its size.  In the graph there is sufficient evidence to say that something happened between the years 2015 and 2016 that caused a significant change in the shift from coal to cleaner energy sources. Other than that we would need more evidence.  I believe that randomness would not affect this graph because of what is given.  The alternative in this article is the mention that the shift from coal to renewable power and natural gas has led to a reduce in carbon dioxide emissions.  This is because they are both extremely related to one another.   I wasn't able to find a null for this article since there wasn't much said and all that was said was related.  This graph used probability by having the use of a energy source be measured with respect to the total energy consumption.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the individuals or the forms of electricity, are displayed in varying widths in relation to their percentage as a whole. For example, coal's starting position from 2001 has a width greater than the starting points of natural gas, nuclear, hydroelectric, wind, solar, and petroleum because it makes up a greater percentage than the rest. However, as the percentage of coal decreases in usage over time, the width decreases and natural gas takes over by 2017. Additionally, I notice that each power source overlaps each other when there is a noticeable rise or decline in production.

2. I wonder what the light gray section towards the bottom represents because it is easy to tell apart from the white gaps and the rest of the individuals.

3. This relates to what energy sources may be widely used and popularized around the community from 2001 to 2023. It could also predict what energy sources may improve inventions that people will rely on for the future. For example, the graph shows that there is more natural gas which can be useful in furthering the development of natural gas vehicles. Additionally, more natural gas than coal is produced because of its efficiency, affordability, and environmental-friendly option, making it a top choice.

4. Powering the Future with Eco-Friendly Energy

From 2002 to 2014, Coal was the main source of energy but has experienced a major downfall in recent years, dropping to only 16% usage. comments.raw_comment:
Headline- U.S. Energy Source Shifts Throughout the Years
This graph shows the different ways the United States has made energy from 2001-2023. It gives us an idea of how much our different sources of energy that we have access to are really being produced to make electricity. What I first noticed was the decline of coal in 2015 and how natural gas skyrocketed. Coal went from being over half our energy sources to now being roughly 10%. Natural gas has completely taken over. I also noticed how little we use solar and wind energy sources. They have increased throughout the years, which is really shocking to see. I wonder why this is. We are living in a such a modern century that one would think our energy sources have become less harmful. Why aren't we using these options which are better for the environment? I also wonder why nuclear energy spiked in 2020 then declined again, and is now shooting up once again. What caused the spike in the first place?  This is very applicable to me and my community. I and everyone around me use electricity every day. Basically, everything around us needs electricity to function. So, it's important to know where our electricity comes from and how it impacts our environment.

Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Shifting Winds: The Current of Energy Production in America” by Ava of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morris Township, N.J.; "U.S. Most Used Energy Sources: Is Gas Rising to the Top?" by Olivia of Barnstable High School in Mass.; “Coal to Sit the Bench": Renewable Energy to Overtake the Energy Giant” by Gavin and "The United States Energetic Change Towards Clean Energy" by Layla, both from Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich.; and “A New Age of Energy! Natural Gas Overtakes Coal's Throne.” by Andres of Perth Amboy High School in N.J.

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article that included this graph, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graphs and where you can find them in the graphs.

The next graph will be released by Friday, September 13.  The topic – 2024 Paris Olympics. 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who lives in a state which uses a lot of natural gas and could produce a lot of wind energy out in the Atlantic Ocean, but has not, and Corey Andreasen currently living in Qatar, who doesn't miss the rains of The Netherlands (yet)!

We can see that in more recent years, coal is out while natural gas is in. Other resources such as wind and solar energy have become quite popular. Nuclear energy also had a comeback in more recent years. We wonder why certain energy sources dropped and what caused this drop. Especially how they relate to events that happened in certain years. In our community, the surge of solar and wind energy has been shown to be effective all around. Businesses can be seen to be running on solar energy, and wind turbines are popping up more and more. Our title, reliable energy resources: what ate and what didn't.

Natural gas went from 17% to one of the most used energy sources because it is easier to access and get hold of also more commonly used now because emits less carbon. We wonder why there is a switch between Nuclear and Coal because it's going up and down and looks relative to each other maybe they are connected. This data relates to us and our community because a lot of our energy comes from Natural gas and this graph shows how natural gas usage has increased over time and how it is quite relevant in today's society. We notice renewable energy sources like solar and wind gradually increasing. Hydroelectic stays relatively static. Petrolium slowly disappears. We want to understand the fluidity of the shapes better; they look very abstract. We also wonder what event are tied to changes in usage of each energy resource. We live in the United States, and our sources of electricity impact our climate and economy.

comments.raw_comment: The graph shown displays the energy source from the United States for 21 years (2001-2023). In this graph, I notice that there are many sources of energy in the U.S, Coal, Natural gas, Nuclear, Hydroelectric, Wind, and Solar, but the coal source rapidly dropped in 2016 while the natural gas source rapidly spiked. While these two sources switched places, hydroelectricity has remained the same at 6%. Personally, I think that the United States stopped producing coal because it is so expensive and natural gas is known not to be as expensive so they started to produce more natural gas to save money.  Living in New Jersey it has been very clear that the energy sources are affecting the environment and I believe that in a few years, it will be rare for it to be cold in NJ due to the climate change these energy sources are causing. Headline: U.S. Energy Shift the Past Two Decades: The Decline of Coal and Rise of Natural Gas

1) I noticed that among all of the other sources of energy, natural gas had the largest uptick in the years from 2001 to 2023. Additionally, the amount of coal was drastically decreased in the same years, which was probably the reason that natural gas became so popular. 
2) I wonder what kind of a graph this is and how those who created it chose to use it as a representation of the conversion between sources. I also wonder what places specifically caused the most change in smaller industries like wind. It would have to be a rural area due to the amount of land needed to house a windmill farm of sorts. Therefore it is plausible that surrounding states of Idaho could have played a major role. 
3) Living on a farm with multiple massive pieces of machinery that are used to run it, I can see the relevance of energy usage because it affects not only transportation but also how a vehicle is to be operated period. For example, some of our old tractors cannot have a GPS system that helps to drive and navigate in tough fields, whilst newer ones can. So that affects how and where we use each piece of machinery.
 4) Energy sources switch over the last 2 decades in the United States, causing an incredible flip in daily life for citizens everywhere!

comments.raw_comment: The Graph represents the power produced by various energy sources within the past two decades. While analyzing, I noticed substantial fluctuations contributed by coal, natural energy, and nuclear energy. There seems to be a slow increase in wind and solar power, but hydroelectric remains at a steady 6%, spiking slightly in 2018. On the other hand, petroleum continues to serve as “liquid gold” for the American economy, but it is scarcely used because of its environmental detriments. In the United States, coal has historically been a significant source of electricity generation. However, its share in the energy mix has decreased over the years, as coal combustion releases pollutants such as sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and particulate matter, a recipe for respiratory cancer. I wonder what the safest option for electricity would be regarding financing and the health of the people and the planet. Why are we not utilizing solar power more sparingly? As the third-largest and wealthiest nation in the world, the next step to bettering the well-being of the American people is choosing to spread funding for more appropriate energy sources like wind, solar, and renewable. In my neighborhood, most homes feature solar panels. This is a testament to the potential of solar energy to power homes, businesses, and even entire communities and a compelling reason to consider its widespread adoption.  Headline: Shifting Winds: the Current of Energy Production in America.

comments.raw_comment:
It is noticeable that as coal decreases, natural gas increases. The decrease of the coal used for the production of energy dramatically decreased after 2014, which then led to natural gas to have an exponential increase at the same time. This shows that there's some sort of correlation between the two, since as one decreases one increases. Since there's a decrease-to-increase correlation, it raises multiple reasonable questions. Firstly, what is the reason for this dramatic change? (perhaps it is more efficient to use in the environment) Why is it that as nuclear energy increases, coal energy decreases even more? Is the main objective of using one energy source as opposed to another due to the efficiency of the energy in itself or merely for the sake of the environment?

This applies to not only my community, but as well as the U.S. nationally. It applies to my community insofar as the energy enables my society to function, without it we would pretty much go back to the stone ages. People need heating, transportation, electricity, etc in order to maintain their livelihood. 
Headline: Natural Gas Rising In The U.S. By Storm!

What do I Notice:
The graph shows the increase or decrease in energy resources across 22 years (2001-2023). Coal was the leading source until 2016 (51% dropping to 18%) when natural gas took over (17% rising to 42%). We also have other energy sources like Hydroelectric which stayed at 6% for the whole 22 years and Solar showing up in 2013 rising to 6%, even wind slowly increasing over the 22 years from less than 1% to now being 10%.
What do you wonder?
How did these changes come to be, was it some scientific discovery or was it found just to be easier to use these other resources?
How will these things change 22 more years into the future? My prediction is that solar and wind power will increase significantly.
How does this affect my community?
Everyone daily relies on some source of energy, in some communities these things don't matter but where I live I see it everywhere, and there are huge gas tanks. My town is where all the “ugliness” goes, so every day I'm affected slowly, i believe soon the energy resources will change to a much cleaner and better-looking source of energy.

comments.raw_comment:
The graph contains information on the United State's various energy sources from 2001 to 2023. I noticed that the size of the blocks correlates with the amount of power that is produced from the following sources during that year. Up until 2015, coal was the major energy supplier to the United States followed by nuclear energy. While the use of coal as a source continues to decline, natural gas continues to rise, now making up 42% of the graph in 2023. I also notice that the use of wind as a source of energy starts to rise in 2007, while hydroelectric energy remains the same, solar energy starts to rise, and Petroleum decreases to almost undetectable. 
I wonder, however, why coal has had such a major decline during the same time period as natural gases uprising. I also wonder if this is due to the idea of natural gas being better for the environment than coal and if that idea is truly correct. Not only this, but I wonder why the rate of solar energy remains so low even though it has been heavily applied nation wide.
This relates to me and my community as, in my town, solar energy has been heavily implemented. Business buildings as well as houses have added solar panels as a healthier alternative to collect energy. Furthermore, everyday we rely on energy to give our homes and electric vehicles power in order to live comfortably. 
Catchy Headline: Electric Touch (America's Version) - The Energy Sources that Fuel the United States

What do I notice?
- The graph itself records the percent contributions of energy sources on power production from 2001-2023. Since 2015, the production contributions of coal have declined while reliance on natural gases has increased. Nuclear and wind power have also risen; the former eventually surpassing energy produced by coal, and the latter surpassing hydroelectric power.
What do I wonder?
- Is our current scheme of energy production better or worse for climate change than the scheme of 2001? Are natural gases worse for the environment than coal emissions?
How does this relate to me and my community?
- We heavily rely on energy to support the comfort of our daily lives. Following the decline of coal, we should continue to find and rely on more sustainable forms of energy production.

Other renewable resources such as wind and solar have started to increase their role. Nuclear and hydroelectric power have remained relatively stable, with petroleum's role in electricity generation remaining minimal. This transition reflects broader trends toward cleaner energy and reduced reliance on fossil fuels. What I wonder is why petroleum no longer has any use and why it never truly had a massive purpose. As for my community, the shift towards renewable energy sources like wind and solar, and away from coal, could mean cleaner air and potentially lower energy costs for my community.

This relates to my community because it can help me to understand what the most effective energy sources are. It also helps me to understand why certain prices have gone up, like gas because it is most popular as an energy source. I want to know why the information is presented like this instead of a more typical graph. A name for this graph could be: What Powers America.

comments.raw_comment:
What stands out to me the most in this graph is that coal and natural gas have been the two main powerhouses regarding how the US makes electricity. Regarding this, I also noticed how coal declined for the first time in 2015/2016 natural gas shot up and stayed up while coal kept rising and declining. I wonder why we as a country do not try and use hydroelectric, solar, and wind energy more often. They are not only less harmful to the environment but they are also renewable resources meaning they never run out. Does it have to do with money, accessibility, or the fact that some things can't be powered by water, wind, and sun? This is extremely applicable to my life and community because I use electricity every single day and honestly could not live without it. At my school, we use electricity for the ovens in the kitchen, the fridges in the kitchen, the smart boards in most classes, and the ac in some classes.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the title of the graph related to how the united states produced electricity. The graph has coal, nuclear, natural gas, wind, solar, petroleum, and hydroelectric electricity. They all have different colors and sizes. Coal seems to be the biggest, however it declines around 2015. Likewise, natural gas grows in shape at around the same time. Some electricity stays relatively the same throughout the years. I wonder what made the different types of electricity decline in usage. Coal might have become scarce, and people started relying more on natural gas. I see solar energy come out in 2012, so I guess that solar panels were invented around them. Wind energy seems to grow, so maybe people started utilizing windmills as a natural resource. This relates to me and my community because there is so much pollution due to cars and buildings. My headline would be: Electricity Throughout the Years

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that until around 2015, the largest percentage of power was produced from coal. After that, natural gas and other methods of power production became used more often, and coal was used to produce power less often. I also noticed that in 2020, there was a noticeable increase in power produced from nuclear energy and a noticeable decrease in coal. However, around 2021, the percentage of nuclear energy and coal used for power production rose/dropped to around the percentage that they were before 2020. Another observation I had was that the use of petroleum for power production has become almost minuscule compared to other power sources as the years progressed.

What do you wonder?
I wonder if we will see the same trend of coal being used less for power production in the upcoming years. I also wonder if petroleum being used as an energy source will completely disappear from the graph in the future because it is already being used so little now in comparison to other energy sources.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because we all need power in our daily lives to perform functions. Fossil fuels are an energy source to power all of our technology from the washing machine to the lights. The community and I use electricity and power every day.

What do you notice?
The biggest thing I noticed was the drastic change in American energy sources. From 2001 to 2015 coal was the US's number one energy source at 51% . Since 2015 natural gas has outgrown coal as the US's main energy source. Natural gas has risen from 17% to 42%. And coal has taken a backseat lowering down to 18%.

What do you wonder?
I wonder what happened during 2014-2015 to change the look of US energy sources so drastically. Could it relate to climate change concerns? I also wonder how this has changed the US's power grid, since many power plants who burn coal to supply power, and having to change with the ever changing energy market how much time did it take for them to transfer over to produce other forms of energy?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because a lot of the farmland around the area have be purchased and or have gotten offers to sell in order to build solar panels on the races of farmland. This is both concerning and easing to me because it shows that the US is making an effort to change its past ways of burning coal and hurting the environment but its also concerning because it may be harming the environment in a different way. How will these solar farms affect the wildlife of the area?

I noticed that coal became less prevalent after 2016 when natural gas came into the spotlight. Solar wasn’t even in the picture until after 2014. Nuclear power has stayed relatively the same in terms of popularity, with a few waves across the years. Wind and hydroelectric also have similar stakes in energy percentages. 

I wonder what outliers or biases exist in this data. Are there any categories that we missed? Are there any forms of energy that are coming out now that could turn this graph upside down and change the concept of renewable energy as we know it?

Clean energy has a hold on everyone whether they like it or not. We live in Michigan (aka the Great Lakes State), so it’s interesting to see what amazing things water can do in terms of generating energy. Water in of itself is a powerful force, so it’s not a big surprise that we found a way to harness that and apply it to more mechanical outlets.

Headline: Gas is the Backbone of America...Who Knew?

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that we have had an increasing reliance on natural gas now in 2023 with 42% of our energy coming from this source compared to the 17% in 2001. I also realize we have used significantly less coal over time as it has fallen from 51% to approximately 16%. I notice that the “sustainable” forms of energy production have not had significant change over the past despite the billions of dollars we have put into sustainable energy programs in the past.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why coal became so much less prominent around the year 2016 and why natural gas came to replace its spot as what we rely on the most for our energy production. I also wonder what we can do to decrease our reliance on natural gas, which is a finite resource, without spending trillions.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because if the government is putting billions and increasing our sustainable energy infrastructure, we will start to see more and more solar panels and wind farms. I noticed last year on a drive to Purdue University the hundreds of wind turbines scattered across the fields. At the MSU campus, I noticed parking shelters that had solar panels fitted on the top to generate energy. I think we will see a lot of this over the past couple of years.

How does this relate to your community?
This relates to my community because most people want to use the cheaper options, which are the most toxic and harmful to our environment. There needs to be a way to make the safer options less expensive.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that from 2001 to 2014, the United States relied on coal for its electricity . After 2014, the use of coal for electricity began to take a steep fall, while the use of natural gas for electricity rose. Natural gas usage in the United States has risen from about 17% in 2001 to 42% in 2023. Nuclear and hydroelectric electricity usage remain approximately the same in 2023 as it did in 2001, but solar electricity usage seems to be on the rise, starting around 2012. 

While studying the graph, I immediately noticed the large dip in coal usage for electricity from 2014 to 2016. I wonder what caused this dip. Was this dip due to an increase in awareness of global warming? Upon taking a deeper look into the graph, I observed that when petroleum usage declined, solar usage became popular. I ponder what caused the switch from petroleum usage to solar usage.

In my community, people are realizing the effect that excessive usage of harsh forms of electricity has on our community. Our community as a whole recognizes that we need to try and cut back on our electricity usage, or at least use electricity in a more efficient and environmentally friendly manner. Some ways my community has taken the initiative include adding new solar panels and creating more windmills. When driving into other towns, I have noticed less solar panels and windmills than in my community which suggest that my community is trying to actively lessen climate change. 

Coal is Only for Christmas

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that in just six years, there was a large shift in how the United States made electricity. From 2014-2020, three major changes occurred. First, the made amount of natural gas overtook that of coal, which had previously dominated electricity production 15 years prior. Next, around 2019, wind energy became more used than hydroelectric. Although small percentages, the change could be considered major considering how long hydroelectric energy designs have been put to use. Lastly, around 2020, nuclear energy majorly spiked, taking over coal, which had begun considerably decreasing five years leading up to this switch.

I wonder why although the graph represents percentages of energy creation relating to the thickness of the lines, what the crossing of the lines represent exactly. I also wonder what exactly lead to these switches in the energy creation.

The information in this graph relates to my community because it provides a statistic that helps a smaller community, like the town I live in, to better understand the energy they use everyday, and how that may compare to the rest of the United States.

"The United States Energetic Change towards Clean Energy"

I noticed that there were only 5 electricity sources in 2002, this number increased to 7 electricity sources by 2014 as solar and wind were introduced as an energy source. The 2 combined make up 16% of electricity in America in 2014 whereas it was seemingly 0% in 2002.

How does this relate to you and your community?
If the same assumptions are made as me within the community, we can reasonably start/increase investing in wind turbines and solar farms to power our school, town, and surrounding homes.

comments.raw_comment:
-I noticed that coal was a very popular strategy to create electricity in the United States until about 2015; after 2015 natural gas was easily the most popular way. I also noticed that hydroelectric, wind, solar, and petroleum all stayed as a minimal percentage of electricity actions across the nation.
-As I studied the graph, there were lots of changing aspects to the graphs which had me wondering about many perspectives. First of all, I wondered why the natural gas production started out so low around 2002 and increased to the most abundant way by 2016. Similarly, I noticed how the coal shrunk down to nearly half the percentage by 2016 as it had in 2002. This led me to wondering how the community decided that coal was not good or logical for making electricity; did they question the safety hazards or did they just find a more efficient way to produce electricity?
-This is related to my community because energy is a utility we use every day of our lives. Most people do not even recognize the amount of electricity we use daily (we use electricity for our dishwashers, showers, lights, etc.). Similarly, in my community I have seen the production of energy by using windmills out in the country with wind, which is an uncommon way to produce electricity, but is a very safety-conscious strategy.
Catchy Headline: Electricity Efficiency or Safety Standards?

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that in the period of 2014-2015 the use of coal greatly decreased, while the use of natural gasses transcended.  In the period of 2004-2006, natural gasses had a drastic increase, while nuclear decreased. There seems to be an inverse trend that when one energy source increases, another one decreases. When looking at the wind, hydroelectric, and solar energy sources, their use hovered around the same throughout the years.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why there is an inverse relationship between sources that increase and decrease. What happened in these periods that caused the switch to happen? Why is coal such a big contributor in 2002-2014, but suddenly drops and allows natural gasses to surpass it. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to the community because certain energy sources allow for things to be created and used, which is vital to evolving technology. As new sources permeate through different cities as towns, it can strongly affect the future of that area and what they are capable of producing. This relates to me, because I personally use these things in my daily life, even if it goes unnoticed. For example, the electricity in my house and places I go to is generated by natural gas, coal, and nuclear energy.

HEADLINE
